papers.title: Considerations for the use of the term “functional anatomy” in the literature: The vague differentiation between “anatomy,” “kinesiology,” and “physiology”
papers.abstract: It was our pleasure to read the interesting study by Gallot et al.1, who investigated the use of a three-dimensional interactive tool for learning functional musculoskeletal anatomy. The authors found that active learning is more effective than passive learning for students with better working visual memory. We consider this finding important, given the relative lack of studies focusing on learning the functional anatomy of the locomotor apparatus. We would like to comment on the use of the term “functional anatomy” in this study and discuss its meaning, as it has been expressed by other studies in the literature. In the aforementioned study, the “functional anatomy” course consisted of four stages: muscle understanding, motion analysis, motion reproduction, and students' assessment. However, can we speak about “functional anatomy” teaching, or about teaching “musculoskeletal anatomy in conjunction with kinesiology”? The terms “motion analysis” and “motion reproduction” (which were included in the course) involve the scientific field of kinesiology and may cause confusion regarding the borders between this field and anatomy. Although the description of relevant anatomy is essential for kinesiology teaching, the two scientific fields are distinct. The term “functional anatomy”, which can be defined as “anatomy related to the function of the body”, is typically used when musculoskeletal anatomy is taught to kinesiology or physiotherapy or sports science students. As expected in a scientific field that focuses on the motion of the human body, anatomy is taught in conjunction with the movements of bones and muscles. Characterizing anatomy as “functional” does not seem appropriate, because the function of every human organ is inherently related to its anatomy. At the same time, every case of motion analysis does not concern anatomy but purely kinesiology. Regarding musculoskeletal anatomy, the educational process involves, among other elements, the description and topography of muscles. Those components of the teaching material are inherently related to muscles function; thus, they are taught in conjunction with it. It is not common to teach musculoskeletal anatomy without referring to muscles function. The relevant courses are typically characterized as “musculoskeletal anatomy” courses, while the term “functional anatomy” is usually omitted. In other words, “functional anatomy” is not a distinct subfield of anatomy, but is an undifferentiated part of it, given that most anatomical structures of the human body are related to its function. We can note that several studies in the educational literature about “functional anatomy” (although they did not clearly define the term) focused on the musculoskeletal system,2-9 and there is generally a lack of educational research to focus on other systems. Functional anatomy, although it is mainly mentioned in the literature as part of the description of the locomotor apparatus, concerns all the systems of the human body, regardless of the presence of motion.10-17 Several articles have been published about the “functional anatomy” of various organs (such as the spinal cord,10 the larynx11 and the adrenal glands12), parts of organs (such as the sinoatrial node of the heart13 and the papilla of Vater14), or even the Eustachian tube.15 Other authors were not restricted to the macroscopic level but were extended to the microscopic one.16 Mortimer used the term “functional anatomy” of the human spermatozoon to describe how its structure is correlated with the physiology of fertilization.16 In any case, when authors referred to “functional anatomy,” they combined the description of anatomical and physiological characteristics of the structures above. Thus, the use of the term “functional anatomy” can be considered as “arbitrary.” In other words, this term was used to replace the phrase “anatomy and physiology” or “anatomy and function” of the aforementioned systems or their parts. Because of the unclear meaning of “functional anatomy,” there is a lack of research focusing on this field. Instead, there is research about anatomy in general, or about other scientific fields, such as kinesiology or physiology. The research which is considered by many authors relevant to “functional anatomy”, concerns anatomy blended with the aforementioned scientific fields. Another fact that indicates the vague meaning of the term “functional anatomy” is the general lack of published systematic reviews with this term among the keywords of the literature search. To date, to the best of our knowledge, there is a lack of reviews about the “functional anatomy” of a specific structure, without referring only to separate data about its anatomy and physiology. In conclusion, the ambiguous use of the term “functional anatomy” in the literature impedes focused studies in this field. It is imperative to reconsider the application of this term in scientific discourse. We suggest the elimination of this term until the scientific community completes a dialogue which will lead to a formal definition of “functional anatomy.” Until this point, we recommend only the use of the terms “anatomy,” “function,” “kinesiology,” and “physiology.” The fields of “anatomy,” “kinesiology,” and “physiology” are distinct; thus, employing vague terms that blend anatomy with physiology, or anatomy with kinesiology, may lead to confusion in the anatomical scientific community and potentially impede future research.
